summary: Quadratic and cubic Bezier point plus tangent evaluation for camera paths, UI motion and projectile arcs.
problem: Unity ships AnimationCurve for scalar easing and Vector3.Lerp for straight lines, but nothing for "move along a curved path in 3D". Re-deriving the Bernstein polynomial at each call site is where sign errors creep in. Bezier is the right primitive when a human authors the shape by dragging handles: the curve is pulled toward the interior control points without passing through them, which is exactly the feel of a handle. Each evaluator has a matching Tangent function because orienting the thing that travels the curve is the usual reason you need the derivative, not just the position.

workedExample.setup: A simple lobbed arc: launch at the origin, land 10 units away, with a single control point pulled up to y = 10.
workedExample.result: The apex of the arc is (5, 5, 0) — HALF the control point's height, not (5, 10, 0) — and the tangent there is dead level, (1, 0, 0). To peak at y = 10 you must raise the handle to y = 20.

useCases: A cutscene camera that swings around an object instead of dollying in a straight line.
Projectile arcs where the shape is art-directed (a lobbed grenade, a spell bolt) rather than simulated by physics.
UI elements that fly from an inventory slot to a HUD counter along a curve, with the icon rotating to face its direction of travel.
Laying out a curved rope, cable or tentacle by evaluating the same curve at N evenly spaced t values.
The underlying evaluator for SplineUtils, which converts each Catmull-Rom segment into a cubic Bezier and calls straight into Cubic/CubicTangent.

usage.codeNote: Position and orientation from the same t — the reason both halves of each pair exist.

apiNotes.Quadratic(Vector3, Vector3, Vector3, flo: Three control points, one interior handle. Cheapest curve that bends; the curve touches p0 and p2 only.
apiNotes.QuadraticTangent(Vector3, Vector3, Vecto: Derivative of Quadratic, returned NORMALIZED — a direction, not a velocity.
apiNotes.Cubic(Vector3, Vector3, Vector3, Vector3: Four control points, two interior handles. The standard curve: it can S-bend, which the quadratic cannot.
apiNotes.CubicTangent(Vector3, Vector3, Vector3,: Derivative of Cubic, also normalized. Feed it to Quaternion.LookRotation to face along the path.

gotchas.title: The interior control points are not on the curve
gotchas.body: Only p0 and the final point are touched. A quadratic peaks at exactly half its handle's offset (see the worked example), and a cubic typically reaches about three quarters. If you are placing handles by hand and the curve looks too shallow, that is why — overshoot the handle deliberately.

gotchas.title: Tangents are normalized, so speed information is thrown away
gotchas.body: Both Tangent functions end in .normalized. You cannot use them to derive how fast the follower is moving. You also get Vector3.zero back from a degenerate curve (all control points identical), and Quaternion.LookRotation logs an error on a zero vector — guard with a sqrMagnitude check if the control points can coincide.

gotchas.title: t is neither clamped nor arc-length
gotchas.body: Nothing clamps t to [0,1]; values outside it extrapolate the polynomial, which diverges fast. More importantly, equal steps in t are NOT equal steps in world distance — the curve moves faster through its straight stretches. For constant-speed travel, build an arc-length table with SplineUtils.BuildLengthTable and convert distance to t with SplineUtils.DistanceToT.

gotchas.title: No allocation, no caching, no state
gotchas.body: These are pure functions on Vector3 structs, safe to call in a tight loop or from a job-free Update. There is also nothing to invalidate: change a control point and the next call reflects it immediately.
